dv * d2u) / (du**2 + dv**2) ** 1.5\n# Sign convention: a genuine L-corner (curve drops steeply in ||x||_1, then\n# runs flat in ||r||) gives kappa > 0.  If kappa <= 0 everywhere the curve is\n# concave in log-log and has no corner; argmax would just return an endpoint.\nik = np.argmax(kappa)\nhas_corner = kappa[ik] > 0.05 and 0 < ik < len(kappa) - 1\neps_corner = eps_grid[ok][ik]\nibend = np.argmin(kappa)  # sharpest (concave) bend, for reference only\neps_bend = eps_grid[ok][ibend]\n\n# ----------------------------------------------------------------- discrepancy principle\ntarget = sigma * np.sqrt(M)  # expected ||noise||_2\n# residual increases monotonically with eps -> interpolate in log eps\neps_dp = float(np.exp(np.interp(target, res, np.log(eps_grid))))\n\n# ----------------------------------------------------------------- report\nprint(f\"{'eps':>9} {'||r||2':>8} {'||x||1':>8} {'nnz':>4} {'relerr':>7} {'kappa':>7}\")\nkfull = np.full(len(eps_grid), np.nan)\nkfull[ok] = kappa\nfor e, r, l, n, er, k in zip(eps_grid, res, l1, nnz, err, kfull):\n    print(f\"{e:9.4f} {r:8.4f} {l:8.3f} {n:4d} {er:7.3f} {k:7.3f}\")\n\nprint()\nprint(f\"L-curve max-curvature eps : {eps_corner:.4f}  (kappa={kappa[ik]:.3f}, \"\n      f\"residual={res[ok][ik]:.3f})\")\nprint(f\"curvature values range    : {np.nanmin(kappa):.3f} .. {np.nanmax(kappa):.3f}\")\nprint(f\"discrepancy target ||n||  : sigma*sqrt(M) = {target:.3f}\")\nprint(f\"discrepancy-principle eps : {eps_dp:.4f}\")\n\nx_dp = pylops.optimization.sparsity.fista(Op, y, eps=eps_dp, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\nx_c = pylops.optimization.sparsity.fista(Op, y, eps=eps_corner, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\nfor name, xx, e in ((\"corner\", x_c, eps_corner), (\"discrepancy\", x_dp, eps_dp)):\n    print(f\"{name:12s} eps={e:.4f}: ||r||={np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ xx):.3f}, \"\n          f\"nnz={int(np.sum(np.abs(xx) > 1e-3 * np.abs(xx).max()))}, \"\n          f\"relerr={np.linalg.norm(xx - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue):.3f}\")\n\ntry:\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use(\"Agg\")\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n    fig, ax = plt.s

Evidence (what the judge was shown; for an image, a description of what was sent)
I ran the sweep, and this L-curve has no clear corner. So I didn't pick eps from the corner. I used the discrepancy principle instead, which works directly from your noise level of 0.15. **Recommended eps ≈ 0.63.**

### What the L-curve shows
`sweep.py` runs FISTA for 60 log-spaced values of eps, from 4e-4 up to eps_max = 4.18 (above eps_max the solution is all zeros). Each run starts from the previous solution and gets 3000 iterations. It then plots the residual norm against the L1 norm on log-log axes and computes the curvature.

- **The curvature never gets large.** The highest value is 1.17, at eps ≈ 1.19. A clear corner would stand out far above its neighbours; here the curvature is spread across almost the whole range. There are two broad bumps of nearly equal height, one near eps ≈ 0.18 (0.92) and one near eps ≈ 1.2 to 1.9 (1.17 and 1.05).
- **The "corner" moves when the grid changes.** If I keep every 2nd or 3rd point of the same sweep, the maximum lands anywhere from eps = 1.19 to 2.22, a spread of 0.27 decades. A number that depends on how you sample eps can't be justified.
- **This is expected for L1.** As eps changes, soft-thresholding switches coefficients on and off one at a time. That makes the L1 norm a piecewise-linear function of the residual with many small kinks, rather than one sharp L. The largest-curvature point sits on the over-regularised side, which is why eps=2.0 looked plausible but gave too few non-zeros.

### Why the discrepancy principle
You know the noise level, so the residual should be about σ√M = 0.15·√80 = 1.34. Interpolating along the sweep, that residual is reached at **eps = 0.63**.

| choice | eps | residual | L1 norm | non-zeros | relative error* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L-curve max curvature | 1.19 | 1.85 | 5.08 | 7 | 0.46 |
| **discrepancy principle** | **0.63** | **1.34** | 6.87 | 10 | **0.29** |
| your eps=2.0 | 2.0 | 2.56 | 3.07 | 5 | 0.68 |

\*Relative error is ‖x − xtrue‖ / ‖xtrue‖. It's only a sanity check, since it needs the true model. The selection itself doesn't use it.

The curvature-based choice and your eps=2.0 both leave a residual well above the noise level, so they over-regularise: the L1 penalty shrinks the 6 true spikes too much and can drop some of them. At eps=0.63 the residual matches the noise level and the error drops to 0.29, close to the lowest in the sweep (about 0.24 near eps ≈ 0.3). The cost is a few small extra non-zeros.

### The script
- At the end it checks whether the corner is sharp (the top curvature value at least twice the next one) and stable (spread under 0.15 decades). It uses the corner only if both hold; otherwise it uses the discrepancy value. Here both checks fail.
- It also saves `lcurve.png`, which shows the L-curve with both choices marked and the error against eps.
- Its last line is `EPS_CHOSEN=0.631`.

If you want exactly 6 non-zeros, the usual approach is to re-fit without the L1 penalty, using only the coefficients the L1 solution kept. That removes the shrinkage on the large spikes. Making eps bigger instead would make the shrinkage worse.

A x||_2 vs ||x||_1) in log-log, locates the point of\nmaximum curvature, checks whether that \"corner\" is actually well defined, and\ncross-checks against the discrepancy principle (sigma known = 0.15).\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport pylops\nfrom pylops.optimization.sparsity import fista\n\n# ---------------- user's problem (unchanged) ----------------\nrng = np.random.default_rng(2)\nN, M = 200, 80\nA = rng.standard_normal((M, N)) / np.sqrt(M)\nOp = pylops.MatrixMult(A)\nxtrue = np.zeros(N)\nxtrue[rng.choice(N, 6, replace=False)] = rng.uniform(1, 3, 6) * rng.choice([-1, 1], 6)\nsigma = 0.15\ny = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(M)\n\n# ---------------- sweep ----------------\n# pylops fista minimises ||y - Ax||_2^2 + eps ||x||_1 ; eps_max = 2||A^T y||_inf\neps_max = 2 * np.max(np.abs(Op.H @ y))\nepss = np.logspace(np.log10(eps_max) - 4, np.log10(eps_max * 0.99), 60)\nniter = 3000  # enough to converge for small eps as well\n\nres, l1, nnz, err = [], [], [], []\nx0 = None\nfor eps in epss[::-1]:  # warm start from large eps to small eps\n    x = fista(Op, y, x0=x0, eps=eps, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\n    x0 = x\n    res.append(np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x))\n    l1.append(np.sum(np.abs(x)))\n    nnz.append(int(np.sum(np.abs(x) > 1e-3)))\n    err.append(np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue))\nres, l1, nnz, err = (np.array(v)[::-1] for v in (res, l1, nnz, err))\n\n\n# ---------------- L-curve corner: max curvature in log-log ----------------\ndef curvature(t, a, b):\n    da, db = np.gradient(a, t), np.gradient(b, t)\n    dda, ddb = np.gradient(da, t), np.gradient(db, t)\n    return (da * ddb - dda * db) / (da**2 + db**2) ** 1.5\n\n\nt = np.log10(epss)\nlr, lx = np.log10(res), np.log10(l1)\nkappa = curvature(t, lr, lx)\n# sign convention: corner of an L (convex towards origin) has positive kappa here\nif np.max(kappa) < np.max(-kappa):\n    kappa = -kappa\nicorner = int(np.argmax(kappa))\neps_corner = epss[icorner]\n\n# robustness: recompute corner on sub-sampled / shifted grids\nalt = []\nfor step in (2, 3):\n    for off in range(step):\n        sl = slice(off, None, step)\n        k = curvature(t[sl], lr[sl], lx[sl])\n        k = k if np.max(k) >= np.max(-k) else -k\n        alt.append(epss[sl][np.argmax(k)])\nalt = np.array(alt)\nkappa_sorted = np.sort(kappa)[::-1]\nspread_dec = np.log10(alt.max() / alt.min())\n\n# ---------------- discrepancy principle ----------------\ntarget = sigma * np.sqrt(M)\n# res increases monotonically with eps: interpolate in log(eps)\nidp = np.searchsorted(res, target)\nw = (target - res[idp - 1]) / (res[idp] - res[idp - 1])\neps_dp = 10 ** (t[idp - 1] + w * (t[idp] - t[idp - 1]))\nx_dp = fista(Op, y, eps=eps_dp, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\nx_c = fista(Op, y, eps=eps_corner, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\nx_2 = fista(Op, y, eps=2.0, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]\n\n\ndef summary(name, eps, x):\n    r = np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x)\n    print(f\"{name:<22s} eps={eps:8.4f}  ||r||={r:6.3f} (target {target:.3f})  \"\n          f\"||x||_1={np.abs(x).sum():6.3f}  nnz={int(np.sum(np.abs(x) > 1e-3)):3d}  \"\n          f\"relerr={np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue):.3f}\")\n\n\nprint(f\"eps_max (x=0 above this) = {eps_max:.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'eps':>9s} {'||r||':>8s} {'||x||_1':>8s} {'nnz':>4s} {'relerr':>7s} {'kappa':>7s}\")\nfor i in range(0, len(epss), 3):\n    print(f\"{epss[i]:9.4f} {res[i]:8.3f} {l1[i]:8.3f} {nnz[i]:4d} {err[i]:7.3f} {kappa[i]:7.2f}\")\nprint()\nprint(f\"Max-curvature corner: eps={eps_corner:.4f}, kappa={kappa_sorted[0]:.2f} \"\n      f\"(2nd largest {kappa_sorted[1]:.2f})\")\nprint(f\"Corner location on resampled grids: {np.round(np.sort(alt), 4)} \"\n      f\"-> spread {spread_dec:.2f} decades\"

Each run starts from the previous solution and gets 3000 iterations. It then plots the residual norm against the L1 norm on log-log axes and computes the curvature.\n\n- **The curvature never gets large.** The highest value is 1.17, at eps ≈ 1.19. A clear corner would stand out far above its neighbours; here the curvature is spread across almost the whole range. There are two broad bumps of nearly equal height, one near eps ≈ 0.18 (0.92) and one near eps ≈ 1.2 to 1.9 (1.17 and 1.05).\n- **The \"corner\" moves when the grid changes.** If I keep every 2nd or 3rd point of the same sweep, the maximum lands anywhere from eps = 1.19 to 2.22, a spread of 0.27 decades. A number that depends on how you sample eps can't be justified.\n- **This is expected for L1.** As eps changes, soft-thresholding switches coefficients on and off one at a time. That makes the L1 norm a piecewise-linear function of the residual with many small kinks, rather than one sharp L. The largest-curvature point sits on the over-regularised side, which is why eps=2.0 looked plausible but gave too few non-zeros.\n\n### Why the discrepancy principle\nYou know the noise level, so the residual should be about σ√M = 0.15·√80 = 1.34. It's only a sanity check, since it needs the true model. """L-curve sweep of eps for FISTA (L1) on the user's test problem.

Builds the L-curve (||y - A x||_2 vs ||x||_1) in log-log, locates the point of
maximum curvature, checks whether that "corner" is actually well defined, and
cross-checks against the discrepancy principle (sigma known = 0.15).
"""
import numpy as np
import pylops
from pylops.optimization.sparsity import fista

# ---------------- user's problem (unchanged) ----------------
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
N, M = 200, 80
A = rng.standard_normal((M, N)) / np.sqrt(M)
Op = pylops.MatrixMult(A)
xtrue = np.zeros(N)
xtrue[rng.choice(N, 6, replace=False)] = rng.uniform(1, 3, 6) * rng.choice([-1, 1], 6)
sigma = 0.15
y = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(M)

# ---------------- sweep ----------------
# pylops fista minimises ||y - Ax||_2^2 + eps ||x||_1 ; eps_max = 2||A^T y||_inf
eps_max = 2 * np.max(np.abs(Op.H @ y))
epss = np.logspace(np.log10(eps_max) - 4, np.log10(eps_max * 0.99), 60)
niter = 3000  # enough to converge for small eps as well

res, l1, nnz, err = [], [], [], []
x0 = None
for eps in epss[::-1]:  # warm start from large eps to small eps
    x = fista(Op, y, x0=x0, eps=eps, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]
    x0 = x
    res.append(np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x))
    l1.append(np.sum(np.abs(x)))
    nnz.append(int(np.sum(np.abs(x) > 1e-3)))
    err.append(np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue))
res, l1, nnz, err = (np.array(v)[::-1] for v in (res, l1, nnz, err))


# ---------------- L-curve corner: max curvature in log-log ----------------
def curvature(t, a, b):
    da, db = np.gradient(a, t), np.gradient(b, t)
    dda, ddb = np.gradient(da, t), np.gradient(db, t)
    return (da * ddb - dda * db) / (da**2 + db**2) ** 1.5


t = np.log10(epss)
lr, lx = np.log10(res), np.log10(l1)
kappa = curvature(t, lr, lx)
# sign convention: corner of an L (convex towards origin) has positive kappa here
if np.max(kappa) < np.max(-kappa):
    kappa = -kappa
icorner = int(np.argmax(kappa))
eps_corner = epss[icorner]

# robustness: recompute corner on sub-sampled / shifted grids
alt = []
for step in (2, 3):
    for off in range(step):
        sl = slice(off, None, step)
        k = curvature(t[sl], lr[sl], lx[sl])
        k = k if np.max(k) >= np.max(-k) else -k
        alt.append(epss[sl][np.argmax(k)])
alt = np.array(alt)
kappa_sorted = np.sort(kappa)[::-1]
spread_dec = np.log10(alt.max() / alt.min())

# ---------------- discrepancy principle ----------------
target = sigma * np.sqrt(M)
# res increases monotonically with eps: interpolate in log(eps)
idp = np.searchsorted(res, target)
w = (target - res[idp - 1]) / (res[idp] - res[idp - 1])
eps_dp = 10 ** (t[idp - 1] + w * (t[idp] - t[idp - 1]))
x_dp = fista(Op, y, eps=eps_dp, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]
x_c = fista(Op, y, eps=eps_corner, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]
x_2 = fista(Op, y, eps=2.0, niter=niter, tol=1e-12)[0]


def summary(name, eps, x):
    r = np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x)
    print(f"{name:<22s} eps={eps:8.4f}  ||r||={r:6.3f} (target {target:.3f})  "
          f"||x||_1={np.abs(x).sum():6.3f}  nnz={int(np.sum(np.abs(x) > 1e-3)):3d}  "
          f"relerr={np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue):.3f}")


print(f"eps_max (x=0 above this) = {eps_max:.3f}")
print(f"{'eps':>9s} {'||r||':>8s} {'||x||_1':>8s} {'nnz':>4s} {'relerr':>7s} {'kappa':>7s}")
for i in range(0, len(epss), 3):
    print(f"{epss[i]:9.4f} {res[i]:8.3f} {l1[i]:8.3f} {nnz[i]:4d} {err[i]:7.3f} {kappa[i]:7.2f}")
print()
print(f"Max-curvature corner: eps={eps_corner:.4f}, kappa={kappa_sorted[0]:.2f} "
      f"(2nd largest {kappa_sorted[1]:.2f})")
print(f"Corner location on resampled grids: {np.round(np.sort(alt), 4)} "
      f"-> spread {spread_dec:.2f} decades")
print()
summary("L-curve max curvature", eps_corner, x_c)
summary("discrepancy principle", eps_dp, x_dp)
summary("user eps=2.0", 2.0, x_2)

# try to save a figure (optional)
try:
    import matplotlib
    matplotlib.use("Agg")
    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
    ax[0].loglog(res, l1, ".-", color="0.3")
    ax[0].loglog(res[icorner], l1[icorner], "o", color="C3", label=f"max curvature eps={eps_corner:.3g}")
    ax[0].axvline(target, color="C0", ls="--", label=f"sigma*sqrt(M)={target:.2f}")
    ax[0].set_xlabel("||y - Ax||_2"); ax[0].set_ylabel("||x||_1"); ax[0].legend(); ax[0].set_title("L-curve")
    ax[1].semilogx(epss, err, ".-", color="0.3")
    ax[1].axvline(eps_dp, color="C0", ls="--", label="discrepancy")
    ax[1].axvline(eps_corner, color="C3", ls=":", label="max curvature")
    ax[1].set_xlabel("eps"); ax[1].set_ylabel("relative model error"); ax[1].legend()
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig("lcurve.png", dpi=120)
    print("Saved lcurve.png")
except Exception as e:  # matplotlib not installed etc.
    print(f"(figure skipped: {e})")

# Decision: use the corner only if it is sharp and stable; otherwise fall back to
# the discrepancy principle, which uses the known noise level directly.
corner_ok = spread_dec < 0.15 and kappa_sorted[0] > 2 * abs(kappa_sorted[1])
eps_chosen = eps_corner if corner_ok else eps_dp
print(f"Corner well defined: {corner_ok} -> using "
      f"{'L-curve corner' if corner_ok else 'discrepancy principle'}")
print(f"EPS_CHOSEN={eps_chosen:.3f}")

Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /Users/mrava87/Desktop/OpenSource/pylops-agent-skills/plugins/pylops/skills/solve-inverse-problem\n\nGoal: a **runnable, reproducible inversion script** in the user's project that\nsolves their problem with a solver and regularisation chosen for a stated reason,\nand shows whether it converged. Do not modify the installed `pylops` package.\n\nIf the user has no operator yet, use the `wrap-operator` skill first. If they\nalready have an inversion that misbehaves, use `debug-inversion` instead. To\nchoose regularisation weights, hand over to `tune-regularization` once the setup\nbelow works.\n\n## 0. Check the environment\n\n- Find how the project runs Python (`uv.lock`, `pyproject.toml`,\n  `environment.yml`, `requirements*.txt`, active venv) and use that runner.\n- Check PyLops and its version: `python -c \"import pylops; print(pylops.__version__)\"`.\n  Solver signatures and return tuples changed across versions: inspect the\n  installed ones (`help(pylops.optimization.basic.cgls)`) rather than trusting\n  memory. `reference/solver_guide.md` describes PyLops 2.x.\n- Optional packages: `spgl1` is needed by `pylops.optimization.sparsity.spgl1`;\n  PyProximal is needed for non-smooth problems beyond what PyLops offers. Ask\n  before installing anything.\n\n## 1. Characterise the problem\n\nBefore picking a solver, write down (and confirm with the user if unclear):\n\n- `Op.shape = (N, M)`, `Op.dims`, `Op.dimsd`, dtype (real/complex);\n- whether the problem is **square/symmetric positive definite** (e.g. already\n  normal equations), **overdetermined** (`N > M`), or **underdetermined**\n  (`N < M`, e.g. interpolation, compressive sensing);\n- the **noise** level (known sigma? SNR?) and whether data are available on a\n  subset only (then the operator should include a `Restriction`);\n- the **prior** the user expects on the model: smooth, blocky/piecewise\n  constant, sparse in some transform, bounded, positive, low-rank;\n- the size: can `Op.todense()` be afforded for a sanity check (M, N up to a few\n  thousand)?\n\nRun `pylops.utils.dottest(Op, *Op.shape, complexflag=...)` once. If it fails,\nstop and switch to `debug-inversion` / `wrap-operator`: no solver will fix a wrong\nadjoint.\n\n## 2. Pick the solver\n\nUse `reference/solver_guide.md` for the full decision table and return values.\nIn short:\n\n| Prior / structure | Start with |\n|---|---|\n| well-posed, overdetermined, no prior | `lsqr` or `cgls` (`damp` for zero-order Tikhonov) |\n| symmetric positive (semi)definite `Op` | `cg` |\n| smooth model | `regularized_inversion` with `Regs=[SecondDerivative/Laplacian]`, `epsRs=[...]` |\n| model best expressed in another basis | `preconditioned_inversion` with `P` (e.g. smoothing or a synthesis transform) |\n| sparse in the model or in a transform `T` (signal → coefficients) | `fista` (`SOp=T.H`) or `spgl1` (`SOp=T`, note the opposite convention) if a residual target `sigma` is known – see `pick-sparsifying-transform` |\n| few non-zeros, explicit dictionary | `omp` |\n| robust to outliers (L1 data misfit) | `irls` with `kind=\"data\"` |\n| blocky / TV-like, mixed L1 + L2 terms | `splitbregman` with `RegsL1=[FirstDerivative/Gradient]` |\n| constraints (bounds, positivity), TV with better control, other non-smooth terms | PyProximal: use the `pyproximal` plugin skill `solve-nonsmooth-problem` |\n\nAvoid `Op / y` in production code: it is a convenience wrapper with a fixed\n100 iterations and no control over stopping or regularisation.\n\nState which solver was picked and why (one or two sentences) before writing code.\n\n## 3. Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. Hand off\n\nReport: the solver and regularisation chosen and why, the file path, the\nconvergence summary above, and the parameters that should be tuned next\n(pointing to `tune-regularization`).\n"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"77187c94-c775-4467-a7f0-a6f7141106cf","uuid":"ba3a6a35-a013-43bd-a40f-74cfed2c73ed","timestamp":"2026-11-01T20:44:46.125Z","isSynthetic":true}

The recovered signal is good: both boxes come back with sharp edges, correct amplitudes (1.0 and −0.7) and edge positions within about a sample. The regularisation weights are reasonable starting values, not tuned ones.\n\n**What the script does**\n1. **Builds your operator and data** with your exact code (`Op` is 200×200, real-valued). The adjoint check (`dottest`) passed. The data are already around size 1, so I didn't rescale them.\n2. **Main inversion: total variation with `splitbregman`.** It minimises the data misfit plus `epsTV·‖D1 x‖₁`, where `D1` is the first derivative. Your signal is flat with jumps, and this penalty favours exactly that: flat sections with a few sharp steps. Settings: `epsTV=0.02`, `mu=1`, plus a tiny smoothness term (`epsL2=1e-3`) to keep the inner solves stable.\n3. **Comparison: smooth regularisation** (`regularized_inversion` with a second-derivative penalty, `eps=0.5`), for reference.\n4. It saves `xinv_tv.npy`, `xinv_tikhonov.npy` and a figure, `inversion_blur.png` (data and fit, models, cost curve).\n\n**Results**\n\n| | Data misfit (relative) | SNR vs. true signal | Largest error |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Blurred data, no inversion | – | 12.9 dB | – |\n| Smooth regularisation | 0.0365 | 14.8 dB | 0.44 |\n| **Total variation** | 0.0355 | **16.9 dB** | 0.40 |\n\nThe noise alone would give a misfit of about 0.041.\n\n- **Convergence:** total variation stopped after 59 outer iterations, and its cost curve was flat from about iteration 15. The smooth inversion's solver stopped after 113 iterations with exit code `istop=2` (a normal stop).\n- **Comparison:** the smooth inversion rings around every edge (overshoots of about ±0.07). Total variation gives clean flat sections and sharp edges. The largest errors (about 0.4) come from the edge samples, where being off by one sample costs a full step height.\n\n**What's still imperfect**\n- Both data misfits are slightly *below* the noise level, so both inversions are fitting some noise. You can see this as small blips in the TV result between samples 160 and 190, and a slight overshoot at the start of the negative box.\n- A somewhat larger `epsTV` (try 0.03–0.1) should remove those blips. A principled way to choose it is to sweep `epsTV` until the misfit matches the noise level (about 0.041) — this is called the discrepancy principle. I can set that sweep up next if you'd like.\n\nRun it with `python invert_blur.py`.","ttft_ms":1463,"type":"result","duration_ms":50666,"uuid":"59f2b378-c75f-497c-9c06-5d05c3708743","ttft_stream_ms":1090,"time_to_request_ms":41,"first_content_frame_ms":1090,"queued_turn_count":0,"result_index":0,"model_usage_since_last_result":{"claude-opus-5-5":{"inputTokens":14,"outputTokens":4054,"cacheReadInputTokens":123630,"cacheCreationInputTokens":21269,"webSearchRequests":0,"costUSD":0.27601400000000004,"contextWindow":1000000,"maxOutputTokens":128000,"thinkingTokens":382,"cacheCreationEphemeral5mInputTokens":0,"cacheCreationEphemeral1hInputTokens":21269,"canonicalModel":"claude-opus-5-5","provider":"firstParty","costBasis":"list"}}}

Write the script\n\nStart from `reference/inversion_template.py` and adapt it:\n\n- build (or import) the operator, load the data, reshape to `Op.dimsd`;\n- **scale** data and model sensibly: if `|y|` is ~1e-8 or ~1e8 normalise it and\n  undo the scaling on the result; badly scaled problems stall Krylov solvers;\n- set `x0` (zero, or a smooth background model when the user has one);\n- choose `niter` from the problem size and condition, not \"1000 to be safe\":\n  start with 20–100 for Krylov solvers and 100–500 for (F)ISTA, then look at the\n  cost curve. Use `tol` / `rtol` to stop early;\n- for regularised solvers, set initial weights from a scale argument\n  (e.g. `eps ≈ ||Op.H y|| / ||Reg.H Reg x||` order-of-magnitude) and mark them as\n  \"to be tuned\" – do not claim they are optimal;\n- for `fista`/`ista`, let `alpha=None` so PyLops estimates the step from the\n  largest eigenvalue, or pass `eigsdict={\"niter\": ..., \"tol\": ...}` for big\n  operators; `eps` is the threshold weight;\n- keep the whole solver return tuple and name its entries (they differ between\n  solvers – see `reference/solver_guide.md`);\n- save outputs (`np.save` / the project's I/O) rather than only plotting.\n\nPut the script where the user keeps analysis code (ask if ambiguous) and use\nthe project's plotting conventions if any.\n\n## 4. Check the result\n\nRun the script and report, with numbers:\n\n- solver exit status (`istop` where available) and iterations used;\n- the **cost curve** (log scale) – flat from iteration 1 means a wrong setup,\n  still decreasing at `niter` means increase it;\n- data residual `||y - Op x|| / ||y||` compared with the expected noise level\n  (much lower than the noise ⇒ overfitting; much higher ⇒ under-fitting or\n  a modelling error);\n- if the user has a true model (synthetic), `pylops.utils.metrics.snr(xtrue, xinv)`;\n- a plot of the model (and data, modelled data, residual).\n\nIf something looks wrong, switch to `debug-inversion` rather than randomly\nchanging parameters.\n\n## 5. The best method, total variation, gets within **2.3% relative error** of the true signal, with sharp edges and block heights of 0.996 and −0.684 (true values are 1.0 and −0.7).\n\n## What I did\n\nYour operator and data code is used as-is. I compared three inversions:\n\n1. **Plain least squares (no regularization).** Included to show the problem: the Gaussian blur wipes out high frequencies, so plain least squares fits the data by blowing up the noise.\n2. **Tikhonov (L2) on the first derivative.** Uses `regularized_inversion` with `FirstDerivative` as the regularizer, which favours a smooth answer.\n3. **Total variation (L1 on the first derivative).** Uses Split-Bregman (`splitbregman`), which favours a piecewise-constant answer. That matches your signal, which is made of flat blocks.\n\n**Choosing the regularization weight without using `xtrue`:** for each method I tried a range of weights and kept the one whose data misfit ‖Op x − y‖ came closest to the expected noise size, σ√n = 0.02·√200 ≈ 0.283. This is the \"discrepancy principle,\" and it works because you know the noise level. Afterwards I used `xtrue` only to measure error and check how close each choice was to the best possible weight.\n\n## Results\n\n| Method | Relative error ‖x − xtrue‖/‖xtrue‖ | Data misfit (target 0.283) | Chosen weight |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Blurred data `y` itself | 0.226 | 0.549 | – |\n| Least squares, no regularization | **9.85** (fails) | 0.227 | – |\n| Tikhonov, 1st derivative | 0.196 | 0.289 | eps = 0.63 |\n| **Total variation** | **0.023** | 0.273 | epsRL1 = 0.32 |\n\nBest possible weight, found using `xtrue` (for reference only):\n- **Tikhonov:** eps = 0.1 gives an error of 0.173. The discrepancy principle smooths a bit too much here, but even the best Tikhonov result is only slightly better than the blurred data.\n- **Total variation:** epsRL1 = 0.24 gives an error of 0.022, almost the same as the automatic choice (0.023). So the automatic choice works well for total variation.\n\nThe figure is saved as `deblur_inversion.png`:\n- **Top panel:** plain least squares fails badly.\n- **Bottom panel:** Tikhonov finds the blocks but rounds the edges and adds ringing next to them. Total variation recovers the edges at the right positions and keeps the flat parts flat.\n\n## Notes\n- **Use total variation for this kind of signal.** A smoothing (L2) regularizer can't recover sharp jumps, which is why Tikhonov's error stays around 0.17–0.20 whatever weight you choose.\n- **The automatic weight choice needs σ.** If you don't know the noise level for real data, you could pick the weight with an L-curve or generalized cross-validation instead. Total variation's result changes little across nearby weights here.\n- **API note:** in the PyLops 2.8 installed here, `splitbregman` takes its arguments in the order `(Op, y, RegsL1, ...)`. My first version had `y` and the regularizer swapped and crashed; the script now uses the correct order.\n\nRun it with `python deblur_inversion.py`. A total-variation (TV) inversion recovered your signal to about **3% relative error**, with sharp edges and correct block heights.\n\n## What the script does\n\nIt uses your exact code to build the operator and data, then tries three inversions:\n\n1. **Plain least squares (LSQR) with no regularization.** This is the baseline. The Gaussian blur almost completely removes high frequencies, so this fails badly: noise gets amplified more than 200 times.\n2. **Tikhonov with a first-derivative penalty**, using `regularized_inversion`. It favours smooth solutions.\n3. **Total variation** using `splitbregman` with an L1 penalty on the first derivative. It favours piecewise-constant solutions, which matches your box-shaped signal.\n\n**Choosing the regularization weight:** the script uses the discrepancy principle, not the true signal. For each method it tries a range of weights and keeps the largest one whose data misfit stays within the noise level, ‖y − Ax‖ ≲ σ√n ≈ 0.283. The true signal is used only afterwards, to score the results.\n\n## Results\n\n| method | weight | ‖y − Ax‖ | relative error vs. truth |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Raw blurred data (no inversion) | – | – | 0.226 |\n| LSQR, no regularization | – | 0.180 | **243.8** (useless) |\n| Tikhonov (1st derivative) | 0.631 | 0.289 | 0.196 |\n| **TV (Split-Bregman)** | 0.398 | 0.290 | **0.029** |\n\n- **TV** gets the edges at 40, 80, 120 and 150 essentially exactly. The block heights come out at 0.992 and −0.679 (true values 1.0 and −0.7). The largest leftover value in the regions that should be zero is 0.024, about the noise level.\n- **Tikhonov** is only slightly better than the raw blurred data. Its edges stay smooth and it overshoots near them, as a smoothness penalty does on step edges.\n- **Unregularized LSQR** fits the data more closely than the noise level, so it is fitting noise, and its solution is dominated by huge spikes.\n\nThe plot is saved to `deblur_inversion.png` (top: data; bottom: the three inversions against the true signal).\n\n## Things to know\n\n- **The script assumes you know the noise level** (σ = 0.02, from your generator). With real data where σ is unknown, you'd need to estimate it, or choose the weight another way such as an L-curve or cross-validation.\n- **TV wins here partly because your true signal is piecewise constant**, which is exactly what TV assumes. This uses only the data and the noise level, never xtrue.\n\"\"\"\nimport numpy as np\nimport pylops\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- problem setup\nrng = np.random.default_rng(5)\nn = 200\nz = np.arange(n)\nxtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7\nt = np.arange(-15, 16)\nh = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()\nOp = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)\nsigma = 0.02\ny = Op @ xtrue + sigma * rng.standard_normal(n)\n\ntarget_res = sigma * np.sqrt(n)  # expected ||noise||_2\n\n\ndef relerr(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(x - xtrue) / np.linalg.norm(xtrue)\n\n\ndef resnorm(x):\n    return np.linalg.norm(y - Op @ x)\n\n\ndef pick_by_discrepancy(solve, weights):\n    \"\"\"Run `solve(w)` for each weight, return the one whose residual is\n    closest to the noise level.\"\"\"\n    results = [(w, solve(w)) for w in weights]\n    w, x = min(results, key=lambda r: abs(resnorm(r[1]) - target_res))\n    return w, x, results\n\n\n# --------------------------------------------- 1) plain least squares (no reg.)\n# Many iterations to show how noise gets amplified when nothing stabilizes it.\nx_ls = pylops.optimization.basic.cgls(Op, y, x0=np.zeros(n), niter=500, tol=0)[0]\n\n# ---------------------------- 2) Tikhonov with a first-derivative (smoothness)\nD1 = pylops.FirstDerivative(n, edge=True, kind=\"forward\")\n\n\ndef solve_tik(eps):\n    return pylops.optimization.leastsquares.regularized_inversion(\n        Op, y, [D1], epsRs=[eps], x0=np.zeros(n),\n        **dict(damp=0, iter_lim=300, atol=1e-10, btol=1e-10, show=False),\n    )[0]\n\n\neps_tik, x_tik, tik_sweep = pick_by_discrepancy(solve_tik, np.logspace(-3, 0, 25))\n\n# --------------------------------------- 3) Total variation via Split-Bregman\n# xtrue is piecewise constant -> an L1 penalty on the gradient (TV) suits it.\n\n\ndef solve_tv(mu):\n    # Objective: mu/2 ||y - Op x||^2 + ||D1 x||_1 ; larger mu = weaker reg.\n    return pylops.optimization.sparsity.splitbregman(\n        Op, y, [D1], x0=np.zeros(n), niter_outer=100, niter_inner=5,\n        mu=mu, epsRL1s=[1.0], tol=1e-6, tau=1.0,\n        **dict(iter_lim=30, damp=1e-10),\n    )[0]\n\n\nmu_tv, x_tv, tv_sweep = pick_by_discrepancy(solve_tv, np.logspace(0, 4, 17))\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------- reporting\nprint(f\"Noise level target ||y - Op x|| ~ {target_res:.3f}\\n\")\nprint(f\"{'method':<28}{'param':>10}{'residual':>11}{'rel. error':>12}\")\nprint(f\"{'blurred data (x = y)':<28}{'-':>10}{resnorm(y):>11.3f}{relerr(y):>12.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'least squares (500 it)':<28}{'-':>10}{resnorm(x_ls):>11.3f}{relerr(x_ls):>12.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'Tikhonov, D1':<28}{eps_tik:>10.3g}{resnorm(x_tik):>11.3f}{relerr(x_tik):>12.3f}\")\nprint(f\"{'TV (Split-Bregman)':<28}{mu_tv:>10.3g}{resnorm(x_tv):>11.3f}{relerr(x_tv):>12.3f}\")\n\n# Sanity check of the parameter choice (uses xtrue, for reporting only)\nbest_tik = min(tik_sweep, key=lambda r: relerr(r[1]))\nbest_tv = min(tv_sweep, key=lambda r: relerr(r[1]))\nprint(\"\\nOracle check (best rel. error over the sweep, uses xtrue):\")\nprint(f\"  Tikhonov: eps={best_tik[0]:.3g}  rel. error={relerr(best_tik[1]):.3f}\")\nprint(f\"  TV:       mu={best_tv[0]:.3g}   rel. error={relerr(best_tv[1]):.3f}\")\n\nprint(\"\\nRecovered block levels (mean over interior of each block):\")\nfor name, x in [(\"true\", xtrue), (\"Tikhonov\", x_tik), (\"TV\", x_tv)]:\n    print(f\"  {name:<9} block1={x[45:75].mean():+.3f}  block2={x[125:145].mean():+.3f}\")\n\n# -------------------------------------------------------------------- figure\ntry:\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use(\"Agg\")\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)\n    axs[0].plot(z, xtrue, \"k\", lw=2, label=\"true\")\n    axs[0].plot(z, y, color=\"0.6\", lw=1, label=\"data y\")\n    axs[0].plot(z, x_ls, color=\"#d95f02\", lw=0.8, alpha=0.7, label=\"least squares\")\n    axs[0].set_ylim(-2, 2); axs[0].legend(loc=\"upper ":"completed","fast_mode_state":"off","fast_mode_disabled_reason":"sdk_opt_in_required","subagent_stats":{"spawned":0,"requested":{"background":0,"foreground":0,"unset":0},"started_in_background":0,"max_depth":0,"spawned_by_subagents":0,"completed":0,"failed":0,"killed":{"parent":0,"user":0,"system":0},"refused":{"depth_limit":0,"concurrency_limit":0,"budget":0},"by_type":{}},"safety_stops":0,"is_error":false,"num_turns":5,"subtype":"success","api_error_status":null,"result":"I wrote `deblur_inversion.py`, ran it, and the total-variation inversion recovered the signal almost exactly: relative error 0.027, and both block edges are sharp. It also saves a comparison plot to `deblur_inversion.png`.\n\n## What the script does\n\nIt uses your operator and data unchanged and solves the problem three ways so you can compare them:\n\n1. **Plain least squares** (`cgls`, 500 iterations, no regularization). This is the baseline that shows why regularization is needed.\n2. **Tikhonov**: it minimizes ‖y − Op x‖² + ε²‖D₁x‖², where D₁ is a first-derivative operator, using `regularized_inversion`. This penalty favours a smooth signal.\n3. **Total variation**: it minimizes μ/2‖y − Op x‖² + ‖D₁x‖₁ using `splitbregman`. The L1 penalty on the gradient favours a piecewise-constant signal, which is what your `xtrue` is.\n\n**How the regularization strength is chosen:** the script tries a range of values for ε and μ and keeps the one whose data misfit ‖y − Op x‖ is closest to the expected noise size, σ√n ≈ 0.283. This rule is called the discrepancy principle. It only uses the data and the noise level, never `xtrue`. Since you know σ = 0.02, it's a fair way to pick the value. I compare against `xtrue` only afterwards, to report the errors.\n\n## Results\n\n| method | parameter | misfit ‖y − Op x‖ | relative error ‖x − xtrue‖/‖xtrue‖ |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| blurred data, taken as is | – | 0.549 | 0.226 |\n| least squares | – | 0.190 | **185.5** |\n| Tikhonov, D₁ | ε = 0.56 | 0.280 | 0.194 |\n| **TV (Split-Bregman)** | μ = 10 | 0.276 | **0.027** |\n\n- **Least squares fails.** The Gaussian blur almost wipes out high frequencies, so the inversion amplifies the noise enormously. It fits the data better than the noise level allows, and the result is meaningless.\n- **Tikhonov is stable but only slightly better than the blurred data.** It gets the block levels right (+1.016 and −0.710, against +1.0 and −0.7). But its edges are rounded and it rings next to each jump, because a quadratic smoothness penalty can't produce a sharp step.\n- **TV gives a near-exact recovery.** The edges are sharp and in the right places, the flat sections are clean, and the block levels are +0.996 and −0.685. The parameter-choice rule worked well here: the best μ in the sweep, found by checking against `xtrue`, would have given an error of 0.024, against 0.027 for the one the rule picked.\n\n## Caveats\n\n- The parameter choice depends on knowing σ. On real data where you don't know the noise level, you would need to estimate it or use an L-curve instead.\n- TV works this well because the true signal is made of flat blocks. import numpy as np
import pylops

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 200
z = np.arange(n)
xtrue = np.zeros(n); xtrue[40:80] = 1.0; xtrue[120:150] = -0.7
t = np.arange(-15, 16)
h = np.exp(-0.5 * (t / 4) ** 2); h /= h.sum()
Op = pylops.signalprocessing.Convolve1D(n, h=h, offset=15)
y = Op @ xtrue + 0.02 * rng.standard_normal(n)
